paper_metadata.title: Quantum Encoding and Analysis on Continuous Time Stochastic Process with Financial Applications

summary: The paper proposes a gate‑based framework for encoding continuous‑time stochastic processes (QCTSP) using holding‑time or increment representations, reducing qubit requirements from O(T log S) to O(n log(τ_avg S)). Information extraction uses amplitude‑estimation‑based quantum Monte Carlo with theoretical quadratic speedup. Simulations of Merton jump‑diffusion option pricing (1024 shots) and ruin probability estimation (1000 shots) match classical formulas but are executed only as simulations.

experiments.description: Quantum continuous-time stochastic process preparation and extraction framework, including state preparation for Lévy/Poisson/Markov/Cox processes and information extraction via weighted integrals and first-hitting-time detection; demonstrated on Merton jump-diffusion option pricing and collective-risk ruin probability.

algorithm.variant: QCTSP framework with controlled-rotation state preparation, quantum multiplication, and standard amplitude estimation

problem_formulation.encoding_details: CTSP encoded into three registers: index register |k⟩, data register |x⟩, and time register |t⟩; holding-time representation stores (Xj, τj), increment representation stores (Yj, Tj).
problem_formulation.objective_function: Prepare |ψ⟩=Σ_{k,t} p(k,t)|k,x(k),t⟩ and evaluate expectations of f(∫_0^T X(t)dt) or f(∫_0^T g(t)X(t)dt), plus first-hitting time K(X,T,B).
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Truncation of continuous distributions to finite support; controlled subtraction and flag-qubit logic for first-hitting-time detection; amplitude estimation for expectation extraction.

problem_instance.description: Synthetic and analytical stochastic-process instances: Poisson point process, compound Poisson process, Lévy process, continuous Markov process, Cox process; applications to Merton jump-diffusion European call pricing and collective-risk ruin probability.

dataset_specification.description: Parameters shown in figures include Merton model with S0=100, K=100, r=0.1, σ=0.02, T=1, Δt=1/30, jump parameters m and v varied; ruin model with λt=0.6, λξ=1, c=1, ϵ=0.001.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Continuous-time processes discretized into n pieces; exponential and normal distributions truncated for finite qubit preparation; Fourier approximation used for integrable functions.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Simulation results compared against closed-form Merton formula, Black-Scholes baseline, and theoretical ruin-probability benchmark; option-pricing figures use 1024 shots per configuration; ruin-probability figure uses 1000 shots per simulation point.

implementation_details.classical_solver: classical random generator for jump sizes due to qubit limits; classical Monte Carlo simulation and analytic Merton jump-diffusion formula (Eq.10) used as baselines
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical generation of some random jump sizes in the Merton simulation due to qubit limits; truncation and discretization of distributions; Fourier approximation of target functions
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measurement or amplitude estimation used to estimate expectation values; comparison to Merton formula, Black-Scholes, and ruin-theory benchmark

speedup_claims.baseline_method: Black-Scholes / classical Monte Carlo / Merton formula
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports consistency with the Merton formula and deviation from Black-Scholes as jump size increases, but does not provide explicit numerical error values in the text provided.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: State preparation: O(n log(nS)) for general Lévy, O(nS⌈S+log(-ln ϵ/λmin)⌉) for continuous Markov, O(n(qF+qG−ln ϵ/|λmin|)) for Cox; extraction: O(LP/ϵ(P+nlxlτ)) or O(LP/ϵ(P+F+nlxlτ+n max(lx,lτ)))
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical Monte Carlo complexity implicitly O(1/epsilon^2) sampling for expectation estimation (standard Monte Carlo scaling)

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not specified; advantage derived from theoretical quadratic speedup of amplitude estimation over classical Monte Carlo
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require large-scale fault‑tolerant quantum computers capable of implementing deep amplitude-estimation circuits and large stochastic-path registers (O(n log(nS)) qubits depending on process)
limiting_factors: Only quadratic speedup from amplitude estimation
Large circuit depth for realistic stochastic processes
Dependence on Fourier approximation and controlled multipliers
No real QPU demonstration; simulations rely partly on classical random generation

notes: The paper is a theoretical gate-based algorithm paper with no named QPU or simulator; hardware.type is therefore not specified rather than inferred.
The Merton option-pricing and ruin-probability sections report simulation shot counts and compare against classical formulas, but no explicit hardware platform or transpilation details are given.

The paper claims quadratic speedup for the Monte Carlo-style extraction step and exponential/quadratic resource reductions in preparation/extraction, but these are theoretical claims rather than hardware benchmarks.
Paper explicitly claims quadratic quantum speedup via quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo (Section 4).
All demonstrations are simulations compared to analytic formulas or classical Monte Carlo rather than hardware benchmarks.
